description: A sample discovery index until the survey (T73–T75) delivers one: real, known objects at their real positions, with class, score and reason written by hand from our checks (T09, T63), not computed. They are the survey's validation set: a working survey must list them too.
method: Positions from web/presets.json and web/discover.json (epoch 2026.0); class, score and reason by hand.

candidates.name: WISE 0855-0714
candidates.reason: The coldest brown dwarf known (about 250 K, colder than a freezer). Too faint to see at short wavelengths, it should only show at 4–5 µm, and it moves 8.1″ a year: about 1.3 pixels between the first and the last SPHEREx epoch here. The survey's first test: if it can't find this one, it can't find new ones.

candidates.name: Epsilon Indi B
candidates.reason: A pair of brown dwarfs 12 light-years away. Our spectrum check (T63) finds no star shape in any epoch and 3.6–4.7 µm about 5× brighter than a star would be: the cool-atmosphere signature a new brown dwarf would show.

candidates.name: RW Aurigae
candidates.reason: A young star still surrounded by its disk. Its spectrum (T63) is about 15× brighter at 4.0–4.8 µm than the star alone: warm dust. It also varies: one epoch doesn't fit a single star shape at all.

candidates.name: R Draconis
candidates.reason: A Mira variable: it swells and shrinks over about 8 months, so at the same wavelength it should look clearly brighter or fainter between SPHEREx passes six months apart. Blink two epochs at the same wavelength. Known (variable-star catalogues), so the survey must flag it and then recognise it.

candidates.name: Barnard's Star
candidates.reason: The fastest-moving star in the sky (10.4″ a year), 6 light-years away: about 1.8 SPHEREx pixels between the first and the last epoch here. It is so bright that its core saturates: a gap that moves with it.

candidates.name: Kapteyn's star
candidates.reason: A star from the Milky Way's halo passing close by (13 light-years), moving 8.6″ a year: about 1.5 pixels across SPHEREx's coverage here. Blink the first against the last epoch.

candidates.name: SSSPM J1444-2019
candidates.reason: A brown dwarf 56 light-years away moving 3.5″ a year, still only 0.6 px in SPHEREx's coverage here: too little to see in a blink. The spectrum is the test: a brown dwarf is dim at 1–2 µm and bright at 4–5 µm.
